passage:
The flood relief camp in the school building had power for only two hours a day, and three trucks were due before dark. Kamal, three weeks into his first job with the NGO, watched Ishita, the camp head, run the evening meeting by lantern light.
“First, my mistake,” she said. “I counted the rice sacks wrong yesterday. We're short by twenty. That's on me.” Nobody had expected that.
Then she turned to the volunteers. “Rekha found the dry storeroom. Salim fixed the pump. Thank you both.” Rekha looked at the floor, smiling.
“Now, what am I missing? Tell me.” Three people spoke at once.
Kamal noticed the older volunteers stayed late for her without being asked. He wrote in his notebook: trust, not title.

qa.q: By how many sacks was the rice short?
qa.a: The rice was short by twenty sacks.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling as he watched Ishita run the meeting?
qa.a: He felt surprised and admiring, noticing how her honesty and credit-giving made people trust her.

qa.q: What does Ishita do that makes people want to follow her?
qa.a: She admits her own mistake, gives specific credit to volunteers and asks for views, so people trust her rather than just obey.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt when Ishita thanked her?
qa.a: Rekha seemed shy but pleased, smiling at the floor at being noticed in front of everyone.

grounding: Shows a junior watching a leader admit mistakes, give credit and ask for views under pressure, and learning trust outlasts position.

passage:
In the bank branch in Jayanagar, Dolma had been an officer for six months when the big client meeting went wrong. The loan papers had the wrong interest date.
Deepak, the branch manager, didn't look at her, though she had prepared the file. He said to the client, “That's my error. I signed it without checking. We'll correct it today.”
After the client left, he called the team together. “Dolma found the fix in ten minutes. Good work.” Then he asked, “What should we change so this doesn't happen again?” Dolma suggested a second check. He wrote it on the board.
That evening Dolma thought about her old manager, who had shouted at juniors in front of clients. Nobody had stayed late for him. Everyone stayed for Deepak.

qa.q: What was wrong in the loan papers?
qa.a: They had the wrong interest date.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when Deepak took the blame in front of the client?
qa.a: She felt relieved and grateful, and grew to respect and trust him.

qa.q: What can a new leader learn from Deepak?
qa.a: Take responsibility in front of others, give specific credit to the team, and ask them how to improve, which builds lasting trust.

qa.q: How might the client have seen Deepak's response?
qa.a: The client probably felt reassured by his honesty and quick promise to fix it.

grounding: Shows a junior watching a manager admit a mistake, give her credit and ask for views, learning that trust outlasts position.

“Okay, team,” said Pankaj, the night editor, at the newsroom's ten o'clock meeting. “Before we start, yesterday's headline on the water story was wrong. I approved it. My mistake.”
Uma, the youngest reporter, blinked.
“Now, the rail strike piece. Uma, you got the union leader to talk when nobody else could. Great work.”
“Thanks,” Uma managed.
“What are we missing tonight? I want to hear from everyone, especially the new people.”
Imtiaz said, “The hospital story needs a second source.”
“Good. Uma, what do you think?”
Uma swallowed. “Maybe we lead with the strike, not the minister?”
Pankaj nodded slowly. “Yes. Let's do that.”
After the meeting, Uma whispered to Imtiaz, “Is he always like this?” Imtiaz smiled. “That's why nobody leaves.”

qa.a: The union leader.

qa.q: How did Uma feel when Pankaj asked for her opinion?
qa.a: Uma felt nervous and surprised, swallowing before speaking, but encouraged to share an idea.

qa.q: What makes Pankaj a leader people stay with?
qa.a: He admits his mistakes, gives specific credit and genuinely asks for views, even from the newest people.

qa.q: How does Imtiaz see Pankaj's style?
qa.a: Imtiaz respects it, saying it's the reason nobody leaves the team.

grounding: Shows a junior reporter watching an editor admit a mistake, give credit and ask for views, learning that trust lasts longer than position.

At the farm extension office in a village near Dharwad, Santosh had just become the team head. His three field staff were very different.
Nikita had worked there eight years and knew every farmer by name. He told her, “You plan your own visits this month. Just tell me where you'll be.” She smiled.
Raju had joined two weeks ago. Santosh went with him to the first three farms, showed him how to test soil, and checked his forms every evening.
Farzana was good but always late with reports. Santosh told her plainly, kindly, “Your advice to farmers is excellent. Your reports are a week late. What would help?”
By the end of the month, each had asked for something different, and each had got it.

qa.q: How long had Nikita worked at the office?
qa.a: Eight years.

qa.q: How might Raju have felt with Santosh going to the farms with him?
qa.a: He probably felt supported and less nervous in his first weeks, learning by doing alongside his boss.

qa.q: Why does Santosh's approach work for all three staff?
qa.a: He gives freedom to the experienced, guidance to the new and honest feedback to everyone, based on what each needs.

qa.q: How might Farzana feel after Santosh's feedback?
qa.a: She might feel respected rather than scolded, since he praised her strength and asked what would help.

Abebe had become shift lead at the coffee roastery in Addis Ababa in March. He noticed quickly that one style didn't fit everyone.
Layla had roasted beans for ten years. When he tried to show her a new timer, she frowned. So he stepped back. “You know this better than me. Tell me if you need anything.”
Samuel, the new boy, was nervous around the big roaster. Abebe stood beside him for a whole week, explaining each step.
With both of them, he was honest. He told Layla her batch logs were missing details, and told Samuel he was too slow on packing.
At the end of the month, Layla said, “You're the first lead who didn't try to teach me my own job.” Samuel said, “You're the first who actually taught me.”

qa.a: For ten years.

qa.q: How did Layla seem to feel when Abebe tried to show her a new timer?
qa.a: She seemed irritated and a bit insulted, frowning at being taught what she already knew.

qa.q: What did Abebe do that fit each person's needs?
qa.a: He gave Layla freedom, guided Samuel closely and gave both honest feedback, adjusting his style to each.

qa.q: How might Samuel have felt during his first week?
qa.a: He was probably nervous at first but reassured, since Abebe stood beside him and explained each step.

grounding: Shows a young shift lead giving freedom to an expert, guidance to a newcomer and honest feedback to both.

Tenzin had just been made team leader over four receptionists at the hotel's front desk.
Mrs D'Souza had worked the desk for twenty years. Tenzin asked her, “How do you want to handle the tour groups?” and let her run them her way.
Akash had joined last month from a village near Shimla. He was scared of angry guests. Tenzin sat beside him on the evening shift and whispered what to say.
Neeta was fast and friendly but kept forgetting to update the booking system. Tenzin told her directly: “Your guests love you. The system needs updating every time, though. Let's set a reminder.”
In the staff room, Akash said, “Tenzin sir asks each of us what we need. The last boss only told us what he wanted.”

qa.q: How might Akash have felt with Tenzin sitting beside him?

passage:
At the preschool in Cape Town, Xin and Lindiwe were building a tall tower of wooden blocks.
“My turn!” Lindiwe grabbed the red block.
“No, mine!” Xin pulled it back. The tower wobbled.
Both started to cry.
Ms Dlamini knelt beside them. “One block each. Xin, then Lindiwe. I'll count.”
Xin put a blue block on top. Lindiwe put the red one. They looked at each other.
“Again!” said Lindiwe.
The tower grew taller than their heads. When it finally fell, they both screamed with laughter.

qa.q: What colour block did Lindiwe grab?
qa.a: The red block.

qa.q: How did Xin and Lindiwe feel when the tower finally fell?
qa.a: They were delighted and happy, screaming with laughter together.

qa.q: How did Ms Dlamini help them build together?
qa.a: She knelt with them, gave a simple one-each rule and counted turns, so they could share instead of fight.

qa.q: How might Ms Dlamini have felt watching the tower grow?
qa.a: She was probably pleased and relieved to see them taking turns and laughing together.

grounding: Shows young children arguing over a block tower and learning, with adult help, to take turns and build together.

Irawati put the door on the side. Noor pulled it off. “No, the door goes in front!”

The rain was coming, so the match had to be only six overs. Hrithik was captain and had one minute to pick the team.
Everyone wanted the fast runners. Vaibhav stood at the end, looking at his shoes. He was the slowest boy in the class, and he knew it. Last time he'd been picked last.
Hrithik picked two fast bowlers first, feeling proud as they cheered. Then he remembered: in the rain, the ball would be slippery, and Vaibhav was the best wicketkeeper in their colony.
“Vaibhav,” he called, third.
Vaibhav looked up, surprised.
He took two catches in the rain. After the match, the fast bowlers carried him on their shoulders. Hrithik thought: a team needs different people.

qa.q: How many overs was the match?
qa.a: Only six overs.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when Hrithik called his name?
qa.a: He felt surprised and happy, after expecting to be picked last again.

qa.q: What did Hrithik learn about choosing a team?
qa.a: That a team needs different strengths, like Vaibhav's safe hands in the rain, not just fast runners.

qa.q: How might the fast bowlers have felt after the match?
qa.a: They seemed happy and grateful, carrying Vaibhav on their shoulders after his catches.

grounding: Shows a child captain, picking teams under time pressure, noticing that a team needs different strengths beyond speed.

Naveen was always picked last. He shrugged and said, “Whatever.”

In the college microbiology lab, Deepak watched the new project team of five come together.
Week one was all smiles. Everyone said “great idea” to everything. Chetan offered to do the extra readings. Nobody disagreed about anything.
Week three, the smiles disappeared. Chetan and Priyanka argued over the sampling method. Two people stopped coming to meetings. Deepak thought about asking the professor to move him to another team.

Wednesday passed. Jin sent a message. Read, no reply. Thursday, the same. Jin saw her posting photos from a concert.
